newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM faces leadership test in India visit.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM faces leadership test in India visit.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina faces a crucial leadership test this week during a visit to India where she is expected to sign a long-awaited accord to end a thorny dispute over sharing water from the Ganges river.
Hasina departs on Tuesday for the visit, during which she is to meet Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and other Indian leaders on Wednesday, her aids said.
At the top of her agenda will be the issue of tapping water from the Ganges, which flows through India into Bangladesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal, an aide said.
"The Ganges (called Padma in Bangladesh) holds the key to Hasina's political future," said Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, editor of Banglabazar Patrika newspaper.
The decades-old water dispute, worsened after India built its Farakka Barrage in 1974 restricting the Ganges flow, has often soured relations between the two neighbours.
Dhaka says the barrage, 18 km (11 miles) from Bangladesh's northern border, deprives Bangladesh of its fair share of water and leaves 40 million people exposed to gradual desertification.
Political opponents deride Hasina as a "stooge of India" because her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, signed a 25-year friendship treaty with India.
"If the water accord fails to materialise Hasina will start losing ground among common people, and her adversaries will use it to try to drive her from power," one Asian diplomat said.

Although Hasina has said the treaty will not be renewed when it expires next March, her critics still brand her "too pro-Indian," a tag they have long tried to use keep her and her Awami League out of power.
"Sufficient flow of water would not only soothe the scorched land but it would also wash away much of the obstructions on her way to the future," said Matiur Rahman Chowdhury at Banglabazar.
Ganges water sharing is considered the foremost issue to be tackled before next dry season begins at end of 1996.

Dhaka said a draft water sharing agreement was prepared during a recent visit to Bangladesh by Jyoti Basu, the powerful communist chief minister of India's West Bengal state, which also needs hefty volumes of Ganges water for its Calcutta port.
Officials said on Monday that Hasina and Deve Gowda were expected to sign the agreement on December 12. They were tight-lipped, however, about details of the accord.
The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), headed by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, has demanded the accord be heard in parliament before being accepted.
"We need to see what it contains, good or bad for the nation. We need to ascertain that the treaty is not a sell-out to India," said BNP seceretary-general Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan.

Hasina is to fly to Rajasthan shortly after arriving in New Delhi to offer prayers at the shrine of Moslem saint Khwaja Moinuddin Chisti at Ajmeer. Since winning general elections in June, she has visited Saudi Arabia and China. India backed Bangladesh in its 1971 war of independence against Pakistan.
